claim: Analysis of CoSMoS data is intrinsically challenging because of low image signal-to-noise ratios.
source: However, analysis of CoSMoS data is intrinsically challenging because of low image signal-to-noise ratios, non-specific surface binding of the fluorescent molecules, and analysis methods that require subjective inputs to achieve accurate results.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' knowledge of the field and is a motivation for their work.

claim: Tapqir is an unsupervised machine learning method that incorporates a holistic, physics-based causal model of CoSMoS data.
source: Here, we use Bayesian probabilistic programming to implement Tapqir, an unsupervised machine learning method that incorporates a holistic, physics-based causal model of CoSMoS data.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed by the authors.

claim: Tapqir accounts for uncertainties in image analysis due to photon and camera noise.
source: This method accounts for uncertainties in image analysis due to photon and camera noise, optical non-uniformities, non-specific binding, and spot detection.
evidence: This describes features of the Tapqir method as implemented by the authors.

claim: Tapqir objectively assigns spot classification probabilities that allow accurate downstream analysis of molecular dynamics, thermodynamics, and kinetics.

evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of Tapqir, supported by the data and analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tapqir performance was quantitatively validated against simulated CoSMoS image data with known properties.
source: We both quantitatively validate Tapqir performance against simulated CoSMoS image data with known properties and also demonstrate that it implements fully objective, automated analysis of experiment-derived data sets with a wide range of signal, noise, and non-specific binding characteristics.
evidence: This describes validation experiments performed by the authors.

claim: Tapqir implements fully objective, automated analysis of experiment-derived data sets with a wide range of signal, noise, and non-specific binding characteristics.

claim: In the example CoSMoS experiment, DNA target molecules are tethered to the surface of an observation chamber at low density.
source: Figure 1A illustrates an example CoSMoS experiment to measure the interaction kinetics of RNA polymerase II molecules with DNA. In the experiment (Rosen et al., 2020), we first measured the locations of individual DNA molecules (the 'targets') tethered to the surface of an observation chamber at low density.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup shown in Figure 1A and is supported by citation to Rosen et al., 2020.

claim: When binder molecules are freely diffusing in solution, they are not visible in TIRF microscopy.
source: When the binder molecules are freely diffusing in solution, they are not visible in TIRF.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of TIRF microscopy principles.

claim: When bound to a target, a single binder molecule is detected as a discrete fluorescent spot colocalized with the target position.
source: In contrast, when bound to a target, a single binder molecule is detected as a discrete fluorescent spot colocalized with the target position (Friedman et al., 2006; Friedman and Gelles, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedman et al., 2006; Friedman and Gelles, 2015.

claim: The number of photons emitted by a single fluorophore is limited by fluorophore photobleaching.
source: The number of photons emitted by a single fluorophore is limited by fluorophore photobleaching.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fluorophore behavior.

claim: Working at the lowest feasible excitation power maximizes the duration of experimental recordings.
source: Consequently, it is desirable to work at the lowest feasible excitation power in order to maximize the duration of experimental recordings and to efficiently capture relevant reaction events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between excitation power and photobleaching.

claim: Higher time resolution divides the number of emitted photons between a larger number of images.
source: Achieving higher time resolution divides the number of emitted photons between a larger number of images, so that photon shot noise ordinarily dominates the data statistics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of photon emission and detection.

claim: Photon shot noise ordinarily dominates the data statistics in CoSMoS experiments.
source: Achieving higher time resolution divides the number of emitted photons between a larger number of images, so that photon shot noise ordinarily dominates the data statistics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of photon emission and detection.

claim: Required concentrations of binder molecules can sometimes create significant background noise.
source: Furthermore, the required concentrations of binder molecules can sometimes create significant background noise (Peng et al., 2018; van Oijen, 2011), even with zero-mode waveguide instruments (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2018; van Oijen, 2011; Chen et al., 2014.

claim: CoSMoS images frequently have low signal-to-noise ratios.
source: These technical difficulties frequently result in CoSMoS images that have low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), making discrimination of colocalized fluorescence spots from noise a significant challenge.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical challenges described.

claim: Non-specific interactions of the binder molecule with the chamber surface can give rise to false positive spot detection.
source: In addition, there are usually non-specific interactions of the binder molecule with the chamber surface, and these artefacts can give rise to both false positive and false negative spot detection (Friedman and Gelles, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Friedman and Gelles, 2015.

claim: Non-specific interactions of the binder molecule with the chamber surface can give rise to false negative spot detection.
source: In addition, there are usually non-specific interactions of the binder molecule with the chamber surface, and these artefacts can give rise to both false positive and false negative spot detection (Friedman and Gelles, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Friedman and Gelles, 2015.

claim: Most CoSMoS spot detection methods are based on integrating the binder fluorescence intensity by summing the pixel values in small regions of the image.
source: Most CoSMoS spot detection methods are based on integrating the binder fluorescence intensity by summing the pixel values in small regions of the image centered on the location of individual target molecules, and then using crossings of an intensity threshold to score binder molecule arrival and departure, e.g., (Friedman and Gelles, 2012; Shcherbakova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedman and Gelles, 2012; Shcherbakova et al., 2013.

claim: Integration-based spot detection methods discard data about the spatial distribution of intensity.
source: However, integration discards data about the spatial distribution of intensity that can (and should) be used to distinguish authentic on-target spots from artefacts caused by noise or off-target binding.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of integration-based methods.

claim: Improved CoSMoS analysis methods that directly analyze TIRF images have been developed.
source: More recently, improved methods (Friedman and Gelles, 2015; Smith et al., 2019) were developed that directly analyze TIRF images, using the spatial distribution of binder fluorescence intensity around the target molecule location.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedman and Gelles, 2015; Smith et al., 2019.

claim: All prior CoSMoS analysis methods make a binary decision about the presence or absence of a binder spot at the target location.
source: All these methods, whether image- or integrated intensity-based, make a binary decision about the presence or absence of a binder spot at the target location.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior methods based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Treating all binary spot detection decisions as equal neglects differences in the confidence of each spot detection decision.
source: Treating all such binary decisions as equal neglects differences in the confidence of each spot detection decision caused by variations in noise, signal intensity, and non-specific binding.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of binary classification methods.

claim: Failure to account for spot confidence decreases the reliability of downstream thermodynamic and kinetic analysis.
source: Failure to account for spot confidence decreases the reliability of downstream thermodynamic and kinetic analysis.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of not accounting for uncertainty.

claim: Tapqir is implemented in the Python-based probabilistic programming language Pyro.
source: The program is implemented in the Python-based probabilistic programming language Pyro (Bingham et al., 2019), which enables efficient use of graphics processing unit (GPU)-based hardware for rapid parallel processing of data and facilitates future modifications to the model.
evidence: This describes the implementation of Tapqir and is supported by citation to Bingham et al., 2019.

claim: Pyro enables efficient use of GPU-based hardware for rapid parallel processing of data.

claim: Software packages that perform CoSMoS preprocessing steps are widely available.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedman and Gelles, 2015; Smith et al., 2019.

claim: For colocalization analysis, it is sufficient to consider the image area local to the target molecule.
source: For colocalization analysis, it is sufficient to consider the image area local to the target molecule.
evidence: This is based on the authors' understanding of the analysis requirements.

claim: The analyzed area of interest (AOI) needs to be several times the diameter of a diffraction-limited spot.
source: This analyzed area of interest (AOI) needs to be several times the diameter of a diffraction-limited spot to include both the spot and the surrounding background (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on the authors' understanding of the analysis requirements and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The cosmos model is time-independent.
source: The cosmos model is 'time-independent', meaning that we ignore the time dimension of the recording – the order of the images does not affect the results.
evidence: This describes a feature of the cosmos model.

claim: For cameras that use CCD or EMCCD sensors, each measured pixel intensity has a noise contribution from photon counting and electronic amplification.
source: For cameras that use charge-coupled device (CCD) or electron-multiplier CCD (EMCCD) sensors, each measured pixel intensity in a single-molecule fluorescence image has a noise contribution from photon counting (shot noise) and can also contain additional noise arising from electronic amplification (van Vliet et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Vliet et al., 1998.

claim: Tapqir correctly detects fluorescent spots in simulated data with SNR of 3.76.
source: In initial tests, we used Tapqir to analyze simulated CoSMoS image data with a comparatively high SNR of 3.76 as well as data from the experiment shown in Figure 1B–D, which has a lower SNR of 1.61. The simulated data were generated using the same cosmos model (Figure 2D) that was used for analysis. Tapqir correctly detects fluorescent spots in both simulated and experimental images (compare 'AOI images' and 'Spot-detection' rows in Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tapqir correctly detects fluorescent spots in experimental data with SNR of 1.61.
source: In initial tests, we used Tapqir to analyze simulated CoSMoS image data with a comparatively high SNR of 3.76 as well as data from the experiment shown in Figure 1B–D, which has a lower SNR of 1.61. The simulated data were generated using the same cosmos model (Figure 2D) that was used for analysis. Tapqir correctly detects fluorescent spots in both simulated and experimental images (compare 'AOI images' and 'Spot-detection' rows in Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tapqir robustly fits experimental data sets with varying SNR, frequency of target-specific spots, and frequencies of non-specific spots.
source: Next, we evaluated how well the model fits data sets encompassing a range of characteristics found in typical CoSMoS experiments. We analyzed four experimental data sets with varying SNR, frequency of target-specific spots, and frequencies of non-specific spots (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of four experimental data sets shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Posterior predictive simulations accurately reproduce the experimental AOI appearances.
source: We then sampled AOI images from the posterior distributions of parameters (a method known as posterior predictive checking Gelman et al., 2013). These posterior predictive simulations accurately reproduce the experimental AOI appearances, recapitulating the noise characteristics and the numbers, intensities, shapes, and locations of spots (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, images).
evidence: This is supported by the posterior predictive checks shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Gelman et al., 2013.

claim: The distributions of pixel intensities across the AOI are closely reproduced by posterior predictive simulations.
source: The distributions of pixel intensities across the AOI are also closely reproduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, histograms) confirming that the noise model is accurate.
evidence: This is supported by the posterior predictive checks shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cosmos model is rich enough to accurately capture the full range of image characteristics from CoSMoS data sets taken over different experimental conditions.
source: Taken together, these results confirm that the model is rich enough to accurately capture the full range of image characteristics from CoSMoS data sets taken over different experimental conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the posterior predictive checks.

claim: No tuning of the algorithm or prior measurement of data-set-specific properties was needed to achieve good fits for all data sets.
source: Importantly, all the results on different experimental data sets were obtained using the same model (Figure 2D) and the same priors (Materials and methods). No tuning of the algorithm or prior measurement of data-set-specific properties was needed to achieve good fits for all data sets.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of multiple data sets using the same model and priors.

claim: CoSMoS data contains enough information to reliably infer global model parameters.
source: This suggests that CoSMoS data contains enough information to reliably infer global model parameters and that the model is not obviously overparameterized.
evidence: This is an inference based on the accuracy of parameter recovery from simulated data.

claim: The cosmos model is not obviously overparameterized.
source: This suggests that CoSMoS data contains enough information to reliably infer global model parameters and that the model is not obviously overparameterized.
evidence: This is an inference based on the accuracy of parameter recovery from simulated data.

claim: Spots can be readily discerned by eye at SNR > 1.
source: By eye, spots can be readily discerned at SNR >1 but cannot be clearly seen at SNR <1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of simulated images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Spots cannot be clearly seen by eye at SNR < 1.
source: By eye, spots can be readily discerned at SNR >1 but cannot be clearly seen at SNR <1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of simulated images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Tapqir's overall performance is excellent at SNR ≥ 1.
source: The MCC results (Figure 4D, blue) suggest that the overall performance of Tapqir is excellent at SNR ≥ 1: the program rarely misses target-specific spots that are in reality present and rarely falsely reports a target-specific spot when none is present.
evidence: This is supported by the MCC results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tapqir effectively detects specific and non-specific spots even when they are so closely spaced that they are not completely resolved.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we see effective detection of the specific and non-specific spots even in example AOIs in which the two spots are so closely spaced that they are not completely resolved (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The spot-picker method is much more likely than Tapqir to fail to detect target specific spots when there is a nearby non-specific spot.
source: Conversely, an existing 'spot-picker' method based on empirical binary classification of 2-D AOI images (Friedman and Gelles, 2015) is much more likely than Tapqir to fail to detect target specific spots when there is a nearby non-specific spot (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Friedman and Gelles, 2015.

claim: The high accuracy of equilibrium constant measurements results from the fact that they are much less affected than kinetic measurements by occasional false positives and false negatives in spot detection.
source: The high accuracy results from the fact that equilibrium constant measurements are in general much less affected than kinetic measurements by occasional false positives and false negatives in spot detection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of kinetic and equilibrium constant accuracy.

claim: Analysis of each experimental data set took a few hours of computation time on a GPU-equipped desktop computer or cloud computing service.
source: Analysis of each data set took a few hours of computation time on a GPU-equipped desktop computer or cloud computing service (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the computation times reported in Table 1.

claim: Achieving results with the spot-picker method required optimization by subjective adjustment of spot detection thresholds.
source: We emphasize that while Tapqir is fully objective, achieving these results with the spot-picker method required optimization by subjective adjustment of spot detection thresholds.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experience using the spot-picker method.

claim: Unlike prior CoSMoS analysis methods, Tapqir considers multiple aspects of imaging in a single, holistic model.
source: A broad range of physical processes contribute to the formation of CoSMoS images. These include camera and photon noise, target-specific and non-specific binding, and time- and position-dependent variability in fluorophore imaging and image background. Unlike prior CoSMoS analysis methods, Tapqir considers these aspects of imaging in a single, holistic model.
evidence: This is a characterization of Tapqir compared to prior methods.

claim: The cosmos model explicitly includes the uncertainties due to photon noise, camera gain, and spatial variability in intensity offset.
source: This cosmos model explicitly includes the uncertainties due to photon noise, camera gain, and spatial variability in intensity offset.
evidence: This describes features of the cosmos model.

claim: The cosmos model includes the possibility of multiple binder molecule fluorescence spots being present in the vicinity of the target.
source: The model also includes the possibility of multiple binder molecule fluorescence spots being present in the vicinity of the target, including both target-specific binding and target-nonspecific interactions of binder molecules with the coverslip surface.
evidence: This describes features of the cosmos model.

claim: Explicit modeling of target-nonspecific spots makes it possible to include off-target control data as a part of the experimental data set.
source: This explicit modeling of target-nonspecific spots makes it possible to include off-target control data as a part of the experimental data set.
evidence: This is an inference about the benefits of the modeling approach.

claim: All AOIs and frames in the data set are simultaneously fit to the global model in Tapqir.

claim: Previous approaches to CoSMoS data analysis relied on a multi-step process that includes a separate binary classification step.
source: Previous approaches to CoSMoS data analysis, including our spot-picker method (Friedman and Gelles, 2015), did not employ a holistic modeling approach and instead relied on a multi-step process that includes a separate binary classification step.

claim: Prior CoSMoS analysis methods require subjective setting of classification thresholds.

claim: Prior CoSMoS analysis methods cannot reliably account for uncertainties in spot classification.

evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of prior methods.

claim: A recent approach used a Bayesian kinetic analysis but a frequentist hypothesis test for spot detection.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2015.

claim: Previous approaches assume that spot classifications are correct, and thus the uncertainties in the derived molecular properties are systematically underestimated.
source: In general, previous approaches in essence assume that spot classifications are correct, and thus the uncertainties in the derived molecular properties (e.g., equilibrium constants) are systematically underestimated because the errors in spot classification, which can be large, are not accounted for.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of prior methods.

claim: Tapqir enables reliable inference of molecular properties and allows statistically well-justified estimation of parameter uncertainties.
